content: Sore mouth is a viral infection caused by a member of the poxvirus family. It primarily affects sheep and goats. Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a serious condition that can resemble sore mouth. FMD can affect sheep, goats, cattle, swine, and other cloven-hoofed animals. Although FMD has not been reported in the United States since 1929, if you observe symptoms in your animals that appear more severe than those of sore mouth, you should immediately report them to your veterinarian, state or federal animal disease control officials, or your county agricultural agent. Geographically, sore mouth infection is commonly found worldwide. In the United States, operations have reported sore mouth affecting their flocks within the past three years. This infection is generally limited to sheep and goats, though other ruminants, such as musk oxen and gazelles, may occasionally become infected. The sores caused by this infection can be painful and may persist for up to two months. Humans do not transmit the infection to other humans. The sores typically heal without leaving scars. Animals can become infected more than once in their lifetime, but repeat infections usually occur after a year and tend to be less severe. Currently, there is no approved treatment for sore mouth. However, the sores can be painful and may become secondarily infected with bacteria if not properly managed. If you experience pain, fever, or notice that the sore is rapidly enlarging or spreading, you should consult your primary care provider.
